jeebench:srcjson:math:jee_adv_2016_paper.solve: P = I+N with N strictly lower triangular and N^3 = 0. Then P^n = I + nN + C(n,2) N^2. Q = P^50 − I, so Q = 50N + 1225 N^2. q21 = 200, q32 = 200, q31 = 20400, hence (q31+q32)/q21 = 103.
jeebench:srcjson:math:jee_adv_2016_paper.hinge_label: Binomial expansion of a unipotent matrix

A.pathway: Skipped writing P = I+N and the nilpotency N^3=0, so the three-term binomial never starts.

followup.stem: The given P has 1s on the main diagonal. Write P = I + N. Which statement about N is true?

options.B: N is strictly lower triangular and N^3 is the zero matrix
options.D: N is symmetric with 1s on the diagonal

followup.why: P − I has zeros on and above the diagonal, so N is strictly lower triangular. One further multiply kills the remaining nonzero, so N^3 = 0. That is what licences P^n = I + nN + C(n,2)N^2.

C.pathway: Took 50×4 = 200 from N and then added 1, as if q21 were not purely from 50N.

followup.stem: Q = P^{50} − I. The (2,1) entry of N^2 is 0, so q_{21} comes only from 50N. If that entry of N is 4, what is q_{21}?
followup.why: 50 × 4 = 200. There is no extra +1 in that entry; N^2 does not contribute to position (2,1).

D.pathway: Used the wrong coefficient on N^2 (not C(50,2) = 1225), which shifts q31.

followup.stem: If N^3 = 0, then (I+N)^{50} = I + 50N + \binom{50}{2} N^2. What is \binom{50}{2}?
followup.why: 50×49/2 = 1225. That coefficient multiplies N^2 and therefore q_{31}; it is not a small adjustment of 200.

jeebench:srcjson:math:jee_adv_2016_paper.solve: At most one boy, team of 4, then a captain from those 4. Zero boys: C(6,4)×4 = 60. One boy: C(6,3)×C(4,1)×4 = 320. Total 380.
jeebench:srcjson:math:jee_adv_2016_paper.hinge_label: Counting with a captain and an at-most-one constraint

B.pathway: Counted only the one-boy teams (320) and dropped the all-girl teams allowed by ‘at most one boy’.

followup.stem: Under the condition “at most one boy”, a team of four girls is allowed.
followup.why: At most one boy includes zero boys. Those teams still need a captain from the four girls: C(6,4)×4 = 60, which must be added to the one-boy count.

C.pathway: Chose the captain from only one gender, or mixed the two cases with the wrong factor 3 instead of 4.

followup.stem: A team of 4 has already been chosen. How many ways can the captain be chosen?
followup.why: The captain is chosen from the four selected members, so multiply by 4 after the membership count.

D.pathway: Counted memberships C(6,4)+C(6,3)C(4,1)=95 and never chose a captain.

followup.stem: After the four members are chosen, a captain must still be selected from those four.
followup.why: 95 is only the number of 4-subsets with at most one boy. Each subset still has 4 choices of captain, which is why 95 is not the team count.

jeebench:srcjson:math:jee_adv_2016_paper.solve: PQ=kI so Q = k P^{-1} and det(Q)=k^3/det(P). The given det(Q)=k^2/2 forces det(P)=2k. The (2,3) entry of Q then pins α, and the two det(adj) identities decide which of C,D hold. Gold is B and C.

A.pathway: Forced α=0 and k=8 without using det(Q)=k^3/det(P).

followup.stem: If PQ = kI for 3×3 matrices, then det(Q) = k^3 / det(P). Given det(Q) = k^2/2, what is det(P)?
followup.why: k^3 / det(P) = k^2/2 ⇒ det(P) = 2k. That relation must be used before any claim that k=8 and α=0.

D.pathway: Used det(Q adj P) = det(Q) det(P) instead of det(Q)[det(P)]^{n-1}.

followup.stem: For an n×n matrix, det(adj M) equals which power of det(M)?
followup.why: adj M = (det M) M^{-1} when M is invertible, so det(adj M) = (det M)^{n-1}. For n=3 that is a square, not a free 2^{13}.
